interactions.summary: A student reads Sinon's self-pitying speech from the Aeneid, and Jiang interprets the passage as proof that poetic pathos can override common sense and admit catastrophe.
The class rereads the brawl between Master Adam and Sinon in Inferno 30 while Jiang narrates the punishment structure and the moral contrast between perjury and counterfeiting.

claims.claim: Jiang says Sinon's long speech works by poetic sympathy: despite obvious danger, the Trojans let the horse in because his narrative hijacks their judgment.
Jiang defines poetry's dark power here as the ability to hijack imagination with a false narrative powerful enough to destroy a city.
Jiang explains that in Inferno 30 Sinon lies motionless in fever until hearing his own name, when he angrily strikes Master Adam and restarts their quarrel.
Jiang reduces the exchange between Sinon and Master Adam to mutual insult, setting up the comparative question of whether lying or counterfeiting is the graver offense.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says Sinon is damned because he hijacked imagination and fed an entire city a false story strong enough to ruin it.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is one of the lecture's clearest formulations of propaganda as a poetic crime against collective reality.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's label for the story-tool that seizes imagination and can lead a whole community into disaster.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture moves from Virgil's Aeneid to Dante's Inferno without dropping the central concern: deceptive language becomes the mechanism that captures imagination and justifies hell-level punishment.

uncertainty_notes.note: The quoted Aeneid passage is noisy in the transcript, but its rhetorical function is clear: Sinon presents himself as injured and trustworthy in order to gain Trojan sympathy.
